title: Humming first
hookLine: hum quietly with a recording before trying the words

lines: WHEN DID YOU LAST SING ALOUD?
cards: When did you last sing out loud where someone could hear? For some adults it's happy birthday, sung badly, at the back of the group. Somewhere along the way, singing got handed over to people with good voices.
And yet. Watch someone washing dishes alone, a parent rocking a baby at two in the morning, a person at a crosswalk with earbuds in. Some of them are humming.
No words, no audience, nobody judging. Humming is the singing people do before they remember to be embarrassed. That's exactly where kirtan starts.

teach.b: Five days of listening. Now five days of singing, and the first one doesn't use words at all.

Some kirtan teachers start a nervous beginner this way, and children in Sikh homes can pick up a shabad's tune before they can read it. You put on a recording and hum along under it, quietly, following the tune.
Why start there? Three reasons. First, the melody.
A shabad's tune can wander, following its raag, and learning the notes and the words at once is hard.
Humming lets you learn the road before you carry anything down it.
Second, the fear. Humming is almost impossible to do badly; nobody's listening for your pronunciation. Your voice gets used to joining in, without the pressure of getting it right.
Third, the body. You can feel a hum in your chest and face. The music stops being something outside you and becomes something happening inside you.
That matters, because Sikhs say kirtan isn't a performance for an audience.

teach.h: SING, LISTEN, KEEP LOVE IN MIND.
teach.b: In the Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: sing, and listen, and keep love in your mind, and sorrow will leave, and peace will come home. Sing and listen, together.
Not sing well. Nobody is grading a hum. Kirtan in the gurdwara is often led by trained musicians called ragis, but the sangat joins in too.
The Gurus' hymns are meant to be in ordinary mouths. Yours included.

how: Many children in Sikh homes learn shabads by humming and singing along with recordings or with family, and kirtan teachers often have beginners learn a tune before its words.

games.why: humming first: learn the melody and let your voice join in before the words arrive.

practice: Put on a shabad you heard this week, or any gentle tune you know, and hum along very softly, mouth closed, just under the recording, feeling the buzz in your lips, your chest, the bones of your face.
Don't worry about the right notes; if you lose the tune, listen until you find it, then join back in.

wordCard.voice: Humming first. Joining a shabad's melody without words, so the tune, and your voice, get ready before the words arrive.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, from the Japji: let us sing.
